The Speed.
The legends say a black mamba can run down a man on horseback,
but field guides say twenty kilometers an hour is about its limit.
That is slower than the speed at which a European electric bike stops helping you pedal,
which is twenty-five kilometers an hour.
There are plenty of old reports of mambas chasing riders,
and the South African herpetologist Johan Marais puts it plainly:
the chasing part is simply not true.
Here's the problem.
The black mamba usually turns defensive when something blocks its direct path home.
It is shy, and in the wild it seldom lets people get closer than about forty meters,
less than half a football pitch, before it leaves.
So most apparent chases are probably a snake trying to get back to its lair,
while a person happens to be standing in the way.
It is not running at you.
It is running through the space you are standing in.
Doug sees a mamba, panics, and sprints away in a dead straight line,

The Home.
Graham Alexander, a herpetologist at Wits University,
says Durban's black mambas often live in the same refuge for years.
That refuge can be a termite mound, a hollow log or an abandoned building,
and in a city the last of those can be uncomfortably close to people.
If nothing disturbs it, a mamba keeps a permanent lair
and comes back to it between hunting, basking and mating.
In South Africa, mambas have been recorded basking from about seven to ten in the morning
and again in the afternoon, often returning to the same sunny spot.
It treats one termite mound the way a cat treats one sunny window.
Same spot, every morning.
The unsettling part is the address.
Sometimes the refuge is the roof of a house, or a farm pump house.
In Durban, the snake rescuer Nick Evans removes mambas from homes, factories and businesses,
and says they are drawn to rubbish, messy sheds and rats.

The Snake Eagle.
The most feared snake in Africa is, for at least one bird, lunch.
Brown snake eagles are verified predators of adult black mambas,
including snakes at least two point seven meters long.
The eagle itself weighs between one and a half and two and a half kilograms,
about as much as a bag of flour.
It waits on a high perch, glides down,
and grabs the snake with its feet, on legs armoured with heavy scales.
That is a bird the weight of a bag of flour,
flying off with a snake longer than a single bed.
But that's not the disturbing part.
The disturbing part is the queue,
because mamba eggs and young snakes are taken by birds of prey, mongooses, monitor lizards and jackals.

The Head Lift.
A cornered black mamba raises its head far off the ground,
and that is its first warning.
From that raised posture it can launch as much as forty percent of its body length upward,
which is why mamba bites on people can land on the upper body.
Adults are usually two to three meters long.
For a two-and-a-half-meter snake, forty percent is a meter,
roughly the height of a kitchen counter.
Males do the same thing to each other in the mating season,
wrapping their bodies together and wrestling with their heads raised up to a meter off the ground.
People watching have mistaken those fights for mating,
which tells you how calm it looks from a distance.
Here's the twist.
The raised head is not the attack.
It is the start of a display that comes before the attack, along with the open mouth, the hood and the hiss.
The snake has been cornered, and it is announcing it as loudly as a snake with no voice can.
Doug has cornered the mamba behind his shed,
and he answers the head lift by rising onto tiptoe, to look taller.
He is now exactly eye to eye with it.
Standing taller is also a message,
and the snake answers it with the mouth.
The Gape and the Hood.
The black mamba is not a cobra,
but when it is cornered it spreads a hood like one.
Doug has seen the inside of this mouth before.
At the same time it opens its mouth wide,
spreads a narrow flap of skin at the neck, and sometimes hisses.
One university species account lists the whole display in order:
head up, mouth open, hood out, a flick of the tongue, then the hiss.
After that comes the strike.
The hood is much narrower than a cobra's.
A cobra's hood is an open umbrella, and a mamba's is a folded one,
but nobody should stand under either.
The strange part is the family resemblance.
Mambas and cobras belong to the same family of snakes, the elapids,
front-fanged venomous snakes that also include kraits, coral snakes and sea snakes.
One classic southern African field guide describes the black mamba spreading its neck into a hood
similar to a true cobra's, and hissing as it does it.
It is the same threat display, coming from a different branch of the same family tree.

Doug took the hiss as the start of a conversation.
The mamba took it as the end of one.
The Second Strike.
When a cornered black mamba strikes, it rarely strikes only once.
It can strike several times in quick succession,
and it tends to bite and let go rather than hold on.
Its eyes are tuned to movement,
and once it is cornered, any sudden movement by the intruder
can set off a whole series of rapid strikes.
On average a single bite can carry about a hundred to a hundred and twenty milligrams of venom.
The biggest dose ever recorded was four hundred.
The strikes come the way a dropped phone falls:
by the time you react, it has already landed.
The worst part is the timing.
The last warning is the one you never see, because the first strike is already over.
Bites to people are rare,
and in one Zululand study of eight hundred and seventy-nine hospital snakebites over five years,
only five were almost certainly black mamba bites.
Nick Evans, a Durban snake rescuer, puts unprovoked bites at roughly three to five a year.
He says trying to kill or catch one puts you at high risk of being bitten.

The Dendrotoxin.
The black mamba's scientific name, Dendroaspis, means tree asp,
and its venom carries toxins named after it, the dendrotoxins.
The first one was pulled out of the venom of its cousin, the green mamba, in nineteen eighty,
and the black mamba turned out to carry its own.
Nerves pass messages to muscles in quick electrical pulses,
and tiny potassium channels help each nerve reset after every pulse.
Dendrotoxins block some of those channels,
and the very first one studied was found to make nerves release more of their chemical messenger.
A second set of toxins, the fasciculins, block the enzyme that clears that messenger away afterwards.
If a nerve is a doorbell, dendrotoxin glues the button down,
and fasciculin unplugs the thing that makes it stop ringing.
Here's the twist.
These toxins are so precise that scientists have used them for decades as lab tools.
Dendrotoxins became widely used as probes for studying how potassium channels work.
One black mamba toxin mostly picks out a single type of potassium channel and leaves the others alone.
Doug is shrunk down into the nerve diagram,

The doorbell keeps ringing.
But the same venom also carries something
that does the opposite, and switches pain off.
The Painkiller.
Black mamba venom contains a painkiller that worked about as well as morphine.
In mice.
In twenty twelve, a team writing in the journal Nature described a new group of peptides from black mamba venom
and named them mambalgins.
They belong to the same three-finger family of small proteins as many of the snake world's nerve toxins,
but these ones point the other way.
Mambalgins block acid-sensing ion channels, which are part of the pain pathway,
and in mice they were not toxic.
They relieved pain about as strongly as morphine,
the mice built up much less tolerance to them, and they caused no breathing trouble.
It is like finding a first-aid kit inside a fire alarm.
Here's the catch.
This was research in mice, and mambalgins are not a medicine,
nobody is treating people with them, and the scientists themselves only claimed new targets worth studying.
The same venom that jams nerves shut also contains something that turns pain down,
and right now the only patients are rodents.

The Long Ride.
Before nineteen sixty-two, people bitten by black mambas in southern Africa were given an antivenom
that had no effect on mamba venom, and fifteen of thirty-five who received it died.
A mamba-specific antivenom arrived in nineteen sixty-two.
Over the next years, five of thirty-eight bitten people given antivenom died.
In Durban today, Nick Evans says almost all patients survive,
unless they do not go to hospital.
